segments.translation: [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} tells of that same matter, through the realization of the dharma of [selflessness]{nairatmya}, in the [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa} of the word “[Ḍombī]{dombi}”:
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the song: through his realization of the dharma of selflessness, Kāṇha tells of that same matter in twilight language, under the word ‘Ḍombī’. Where he says ‘that same matter’, the Tibetan translation has ‘the meaning of reality’.

flags.note: tam evārtham, ‘that same matter’, which I took to point back to the preceding song, is de kho na nyid kyi don in the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293), most naturally ‘the meaning of reality’ (tattvārtha), though de kho na nyid could also be a literal ‘that very’. The Tibetan may reflect a reading tattvārtham. I translate the printed Sanskrit.

nairātmadharma: the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has bdag med pa'i chos, with the abstract bdag med pa (‘selflessness’) rather than the goddess's name bdag med ma. This supports my ‘the dharma of selflessness’, marked as nairatmya, although the glossary files the form under nairatma. The Tibetan makes the phrase describe Kāṇha (bdag med pa'i chos khong du chud pa nag po spyod pa'i zhabs, ‘Kṛṣṇapāda, who has realized the dharma of selflessness’); the Sanskrit instrumental adhigamena, ‘through the realization’, allows this.

sandhyābhāsayā (for sandhyābhāṣayā; s for ṣ is usual in this manuscript) is translated ‘twilight language’ per the glossary. The Tibetan translation renders it dgongs pa'i skad, ‘language of intention’, reading sandhā/saṃdhā, and renders ḍombīśabda as g.yung mo'i sgra, ‘the word g.yung mo’. Its name for Kṛṣṇapāda here is nag po spyod pa'i zhabs.

segments.translit: nagarītyādi aspṛśayogatvāt ḍombīti pariśuddhāvadhūtī nairātmā boddhavyā| brahmaṇeti brahmahūṃkārabījajātaṃ capalayogatvāt cittavaṭukaṃ| asampradāyayogināṃ bodhicittaṃ saṃvṛttiśukrarūpaṃ maṇimūlāt viramānandāt spṛṣṭvā spṛṣṭvā gacchasi| bho nairātmā| nagariketi[17]| rūpādiviṣayasamūhaṃ boddhavyaṃ| tasya bāhye| indriyāṇā[m]agocaratvena gurusampradāyāt tavāgāraṃ mahāsukhacakraṃ mayā siddhācāryyeṇa kṛṣṇapādenāvagatamiti|
segments.translation: “Outside the [town]{town}…” and so on. Because she is not to be touched, “[Ḍombī]{dombi}” is to be understood as [Nairātmā]{nairatma}, the purified [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}. “[Brahmin]{brahmin}” means the brahmin boy that is the [mind]{citta}: born from the seed syllable HŪṂ, which is brahma, and a boy because it is restless. The [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta} of [yogis]{yogi} who lack the [guru's lineage]{guru-sampradaya}, which in [conventional]{samvrti} terms has the form of semen, you touch and touch, from the [root of the jewel]{manimula}, from the [joy of cessation]{viramananda}, and go, O [Nairātmā]{nairatma}. “[Town]{town}” is to be understood as the mass of [sense objects]{visaya} beginning with visible form. Outside it. Your house, the [wheel of great bliss]{mahasukha-cakra}, being beyond the range of the senses, I, the [siddha]{siddha} master [Kāṇha]{p-kanha}, have come to know through the [guru's lineage]{guru-sampradaya}.
segments.note: Munidatta reads Ḍombī as Nairātmā, the purified avadhūtī, untouchable; the brahmin as the restless mind, born from the syllable HŪṂ; the town as the mass of sense objects; her hut outside it as the wheel of great bliss, known through the guru's lineage. She touches the bodhicitta of yogis without that lineage (the Tibetan: of the instructed yogin).

equations.en: Nairātmā, the purified avadhūtī (so called because she is not to be touched)
the mind as a restless brahmin boy (cittavaṭuka), born from the seed syllable HŪṂ, which is brahma
the mass of sense objects beginning with visible form
the wheel of great bliss, beyond the range of the senses

flags.note: asampradāyayogināṃ, ‘of yogis who lack the (guru's) lineage’: the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads it positively, man ngag thob pa'i rnal 'byor pas, ‘by the yogin who has obtained the instruction’, with no negation. On the Tibetan reading the bodhicitta is that of the properly instructed yogin; on the printed Sanskrit it is that of yogis without the lineage, which may anticipate the unpurified Ḍombī of m8 (gurusampradāyavihīnasya). I translate the printed negative; the reviewer should decide whether the a- is a corruption.

Divergence, not harmonized: Munidatta renders 1b with a second-person verb (spṛṣṭvā spṛṣṭvā gacchasi, ‘you touch and touch and go’) addressed to Nairātmā, so Ḍombī is the one who goes; the song has so bāhma … yāi, ‘that brahmin goes’. The Tibetan translation has the same split: its commentary says khyod 'gro, ‘you go’, while its version of the song line has 'gro de bram ze'i bu, ‘that brahmin boy goes’. His spṛṣṭvā spṛṣṭvā (Tibetan reg kyin reg kyin) supports the draft's ‘touching and touching’.

maṇimūlāt viramānandāt: two ablatives. Before, I took them in apposition (‘from the root of the jewel, the joy of cessation’) and entered an equation. I now translate them literally (‘from the root of the jewel, from the joy of cessation’) and drop the equation, because the Tibetan translation construes them differently: nor bu'i rtsa ba las dga' bral la reg kyin reg kyin, ‘from the root of the jewel, touching and touching the joy of cessation’, which makes the joy of cessation what is touched. Neither says what the touching does to the bodhicitta.

The Tibetan translation joins the vocative to the next lemma, kye bdag med ma'i grong khyer la zhes so, ‘O, to Nairātmā's town’, where the edition has bho nairātmā| nagarikā iti|. It then has de phyi rol gyi gzugs la sogs pa'i tshogs, ‘the mass of outer form and so on’, with no word for viṣaya and no separate ‘outside it’ (tasya bāhye); phyi rol may render bāhya. I translate the printed text and keep ‘Outside it.’ as its own clause (it may run on into the next sentence).

brahmahūṃkārabījajātaṃ: ‘born from the seed syllable HŪṂ, which is brahma’. The Tibetan translation supports this (bram ze hUM yig gi sa bon las skyes pa, ‘born from the seed of the syllable HŪṂ, the brahmin’) and turns cittavaṭukaṃ into a sentence with capalayogatvāt as its reason: g.yo ba'i sbyor ba las sems ni bram ze'i bu'o, ‘because it is bound up with restlessness, the mind is the brahmin boy’. The Tibetan version of song line 1b also has bram ze'i bu, ‘brahmin boy’, for bāhma nāṛiā, so Munidatta's vaṭuka (‘lad, young brahmin’) may be his gloss on nāṛiā, which the draft renders ‘shaven-headed’.
Minor slips translated through: aspṛśa for aspṛśya (Tibetan mi reg pa); bho nairātmā (nominative) for the vocative nairātme; saṃvṛtti for saṃvṛti. The folio number [17] is not rendered.

Tibetan renderings worth recording for the glossary: avadhūtī is transliterated (a wa d+hU tI), not translated as kun 'dar ma; gurusampradāya is bla ma'i man ngag, ‘the guru's instruction’; siddhācārya is grub pa'i slob dpon, not grub thob; agāra, ‘house’ (for the song's hut), is khyim, as in the Tibetan song line 1a.

segments.translit:
alo ḍombi ityādi| bho ḍombi nairātme tvayā saha mayā abhiṣvaṅgaḥ karttavyaḥ| yādṛśasvabhāvastādṛśo nirghṛṇo lajjādidoṣarahito'ham| tenāhaṃ satataṃ nirantara[ṃ] gṛhītvā prajñopāyātmikāṃ mahāmudrāṃ siddhiṃ labhe|
tathā ca śrīhevajre—
prajñopāyātmakaṃ tantraṃ tanme nigaditaṃ śṛṇu|
segments.translation: “Hey [Ḍombī]{dombi}…” and so on. O [Ḍombī]{dombi}, [Nairātmā]{nairatma}, I must embrace you. As my nature is, so I am: [without disgust]{nirghrna}, free of faults such as shame. So, holding on constantly and without a break, I attain the [accomplishment]{siddhi} of [Mahāmudrā]{mahamudra}, whose nature is [wisdom and means]{prajnopaya}. And so in the glorious [Hevajra]{tx-hevajra}: “Hear from me the tantra whose nature is [wisdom and means]{prajnopaya}, as I declare it.”
segments.note: Munidatta hears Kāṇha address Nairātmā as Ḍombī: he must embrace her. ‘Without disgust’ means free of faults such as shame. Holding on constantly, without a break, he attains the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā, whose nature is wisdom and means, words Munidatta echoes from the Hevajra's description of itself.

equations.en: Nairātmā
free of faults such as shame

flags.note: abhiṣvaṅgaḥ kartavyaḥ: before, ‘I must be closely joined with you’, with ‘embrace’ as an alternative. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has mngon par 'khyud par bya'o, ‘shall embrace’, so I now render ‘I must embrace you’. abhiṣvaṅga can also mean ‘intense attachment’.

yādṛśasvabhāvas tādṛśo: I read ‘as my nature is, so I am’ (‘my’ supplied). It could instead mean ‘of the same nature (as you)’, glossing the song's toe sama. The Tibetan translation has a third reading: gang dang 'dra ba'i gnas de dang 'dra ba dag la, ‘in whatever sort of place, in places like that’, with gnas, ‘place, state’, where the Sanskrit has svabhāva; that is, wherever he is, he is free of revulsion. It may reflect a different reading (sthāna?). I keep the printed text.

The Tibetan translation makes nirghṛṇa one of the listed faults: skyug bro ba dang ngo tsha ba la sogs pa'i skyon dang bral ba, ‘free of faults such as revulsion and shame’. The printed Sanskrit has two predicates (nirghṛṇo lajjādidoṣarahitaḥ); the sense is the same.
gṛhītvā has no expressed object (presumably Nairātmā, glossing the song's lāga); the Tibetan 'dzin pas has none either. I leave it as ‘holding on’.
The Tibetan reverses prajñopāya to thabs dang shes rab, ‘means and wisdom’, here and in the Hevajra line, and names the tantra dpal dgyes pa'i rdo rje. Neither changes the translation.

segments.translit:
dvitīyapadenābhyāsasthānamāha—
eka so ityādi| padmaikaṃ nirmmāṇacakraṃ catuḥṣaṣṭidalayuktaṃ tatra sthitvā bhagavatyā nairātmayā saha ekarasatayā mahārāgānandasundaro hi kṛṣṇācāryyo nṛtyati|
tathā ca śrīhevajre—
nāṭyaṃ kuru herukarūpeṇānusmṛtiśrutiyogataḥ|
segments.translation: With the second [verse]{pada} he states the place of practice: “A single…” and so on. The single [lotus]{lotus} is the [wheel of emanation]{nirmana-cakra}, with sixty-four petals. Standing there, together with the Blessed Lady [Nairātmā]{nairatma}, in [one taste]{ekarasa}, Master [Kāṇha]{p-kanha}, lovely with the [joy]{ananda} of great passion, dances. And so in the glorious [Hevajra]{tx-hevajra}: “Dance in the form of [Heruka]{p-heruka}, by way of recollection and hearing.”
segments.note: Munidatta takes this verse as naming the place of practice. The single lotus is the wheel of emanation, with sixty-four petals (the Tibetan: a lotus in that wheel). Where the song has Ḍombī dance, he has Kāṇha dance there, in one taste with the Blessed Lady Nairātmā, lovely with the joy of great passion, citing the Hevajra.

equations.en: the wheel of emanation, with sixty-four petals

flags.note: Divergence, not harmonized: in the song (3b) Ḍombī climbs the lotus and dances; Munidatta says Kṛṣṇācārya dances there with Nairātmā. The Tibetan translation's commentary agrees with the Sanskrit (nag po spyod pa pa gar byed do), while its version of the song line, like the Bengali, has Ḍombī dance (der gnas g.yung mo gar byed). The Tibetan attaches ‘dwelling there’ to the goddess (de la gnas pa'i bcom ldan 'das bdag med ma, ‘the Blessed Lady Nairātmā who dwells there’), echoing its song line; in the Sanskrit the gerund tatra sthitvā belongs with Kṛṣṇācārya, the subject of nṛtyati.

padmaikaṃ nirmāṇacakraṃ equates the single lotus with the wheel of emanation. The Tibetan translation instead places the lotus in the wheel: sprul pa'i 'khor lor pad+ma 'dab ma drug cu rtsa bzhi dang ldan pa, ‘in the wheel of emanation, a lotus with sixty-four petals’. I keep the equation, since the Sanskrit is clear; the glossary's reading of the lotus might note the Tibetan.

Hevajra line: anusmṛtiśrutiyogataḥ is unclear. I render ‘by way of recollection and hearing’; alternatives are ‘through the yoga of recollection and hearing’ or, taking śruti in its musical sense, ‘in time with the music’. The Tibetan translation has rjes dran thob pa sbyor ba las, roughly ‘from the union of recollection and attainment’, with thob pa where the Sanskrit has śruti, which does not settle it. Munidatta names the Hevajra; I have not checked where the line stands in it.

The edition prints sundarohi; I read sundaro hi (emphatic particle), untranslated; the Tibetan shin tu yid du 'ong ba, ‘exceedingly lovely’, confirms sundara. Pada count: the Tibetan also says rkang pa gnyis pa, ‘second verse’, for couplet 3, leaving the refrain out.

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena nairātmādhigamaṃ dṛḍhīkaroti| hañcū lo ityādi| bho nairātme sadbhāvena svarūpāśayena tvāṃ pṛcchāmyahaṃ sarvvadharmmanairā[17ka]tmayā kasya saṃvṛttibodhicitta[ttā]naukāmārgeṇa yātāyātaṃ karoṣi na karoṣītyarthaḥ| sarvvasahajamayatveneti|
tathā ca śrīhevajre—
tasmāt sahajaṃ jagat sarvvaṃ sahajaṃ svarūpamucyate|
svarūpameva nirvvāṇaṃ viśuddhākāracetasā||
segments.translation: With the third [verse]{pada} he makes firm the realization of [Nairātmā]{nairatma}. “Hey…” and so on. O [Nairātmā]{nairatma}, I ask you in good faith, that is, with an intention set on the [true nature]{svarupa}: given the [selflessness]{nairatmya} of all phenomena, by the route of whose [boat]{boat} of [conventional]{samvrti} [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta} do you come and go? The sense is: you do not, because all things are made of the [innate]{sahaja}. And so in the glorious [Hevajra]{tx-hevajra}: “Therefore the whole world is [innate]{sahaja}; the [innate]{sahaja} is called the [true nature]{svarupa}. The [true nature]{svarupa} itself is [nirvāṇa]{nirvana}, for a mind whose aspect is pure.”
segments.note: Munidatta says this verse confirms the realization of Nairātmā. Asking in good faith means asking with intent on the true nature. The boat is conventional bodhicitta; the question ‘in whose boat do you come and go?’ implies she does not, since all phenomena are selfless and everything is made of the innate, as the Hevajra verse says.

equations.en: conventional bodhicitta, the boat on whose route she comes and goes
Nairātmā
an intention set on the true nature

citations.quoted: tasmāt sahajaṃ jagat sarvvaṃ sahajaṃ svarūpamucyate| svarūpameva nirvvāṇaṃ viśuddhākāracetasā||

flags.note: The pratīka hañcū lo does not match the song's hālo ḍombī (4a). The Tibetan translation's lemma is kye'i khyod, ‘Hey, you’, the same lemma it gives for tu lo in m7 (song 6a tu lo ḍombī, Tibetan kye khyod g.yung mo), so its translators seem to have read a pronoun ‘you’ in the pratīka; it may be a corruption of a tu lo-type opening rather than of hālo. I translate ‘Hey…’ to match the draft of 4a.

saṃvṛtibodhicittanaukāmārgeṇa: before, ‘by way of whose boat of conventional bodhicitta’. The Tibetan translation has kun rdzob byang chub kyi sems kyi gru'i lam gyis, ‘by the route of the boat of conventional bodhicitta’, taking mārga as the course of the boat, not as a separate ‘path’; I now render ‘by the route of whose boat of conventional bodhicitta’. This supports ‘the boat is conventional bodhicitta’ over the glossary's ‘the path of conventional bodhicitta’ (see questions).

svarūpāśayena, glossing sadbhāvena: ‘with an intention set on the true nature’. The Tibetan fuses the two words, bden pa'i dngos po'i rang bzhin gyi bsam pas, ‘with the thought of the nature of the true thing’, reading sadbhāva as ‘true being’; this supports taking svarūpa as ‘true nature’ rather than a plain ‘with genuine intent’.

karoṣi na karoṣīty arthaḥ: I take the question as rhetorical, ‘you do not’. The Tibetan translation supports this: khyod kyis 'gro ba dang 'ong ba byed pa khyod kyis mi byed do zhes pa'i don, ‘the meaning is: the coming and going you do, you do not do’.

bodhicitta[ttā]naukā: Shastri's bracketed ‘ttā’ is unclear (perhaps bodhicittā naukā); it does not change the sense. For sarvvadharmmanairātmayā the Tibetan chos thams cad bdag med pa has the abstract ‘selflessness of all phenomena’ (not the goddess), as I render it, though its syntax (de'i gang gis) is loose. In the Hevajra verse the Tibetan ends rnam dag rnam pa'i sems nyid do, ‘is the very mind of pure aspect’, making viśuddhākāracetasā an identity; I keep the Sanskrit instrumental, ‘for a mind whose aspect is pure’.

segments.translit:
caturthapadena nairātmadharmmasvarūpamāha—
tāntītyādi| tantrīti bhagaṃ padmasthānaṃ avidyārūpaṃ| cāṅgitamityādi| tasya pallavaṃ ṣiṣayābhāsaṃ| etayoḥ śrīgurupādaprasādānma(tma)ma vikrayaṇaṃ parityāgaṃ karoṣi(si) bho ḍombi nairātme| ataeva naṭavat saṃsārapeṭakaṃ mayā parityaktaṃ tavāntareṇeti|
segments.translation: With the fourth [verse]{pada} he states the [true nature]{svarupa} of the dharma of [selflessness]{nairatmya}: “[Ḍombī]{dombi} sells [cord]{tanti}…” and so on. “[Cord]{tanti}” means the [bhaga]{bhaga}, the place of the [lotus]{lotus}, which has the form of [ignorance]{avidya}. “…no more baskets…” and so on: its petals, the [appearance]{abhasa} of [sense objects]{visaya}. Through the grace of my revered [guru]{guru}, O [Ḍombī]{dombi}, [Nairātmā]{nairatma}, you sell these two, that is, you give them up. That is why, like a performer, I have given up the basket of [saṃsāra]{samsara} for your sake.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the cord Ḍombī sells as the bhaga, the female organ, place of the lotus, having the form of ignorance; the baskets as its petals, the appearance of sense objects. By the guru's grace Nairātmā sells, that is, gives up, both; so Kāṇha, like a performer, has given up the basket of saṃsāra.

equations.en: the bhaga, the place of the lotus, which has the form of ignorance
its petals (pallava), the appearance of sense objects
giving up
the basket of saṃsāra
Nairātmā

flags.note: cāṅgitam (song caṅgatā) and its gloss pallava: before, ‘offshoot’, flagged as a divergence from the draft's ‘baskets’. The Tibetan translation renders the word me tog stegs, ‘flower-stand, flower tray’, both in song line 5a and in this lemma, and pallava as 'dab ma, ‘leaf, petal’: me tog stegs ni de'i 'dab mar yul gyi snang ba'o, ‘the flower-stand: as its petals, the appearance of objects’. With the lotus just named, I now render pallava ‘petals’ (it also means ‘young leaves, shoot’). If caṅgatā is a flower basket, as the draft and the Tibetan suggest, the divergence largely disappears. The song's abara nā (‘no more’) is not glossed.

prasādānma(tma)ma: I read prasādān mama and take mama with the guru (‘my revered guru’). The Tibetan translation has bdag nyid 'tshong ba, ‘selling oneself’ (or ‘the selling itself’), which together with Shastri's parenthetical (tma) points to a reading ātma-vikrayaṇa: ‘by the guru's grace, you give up the selling of yourself’, or ‘your own selling of these two is giving them up’. The equation selling = giving up stands either way. The Tibetan also has an imperative, khyod kyis yongs su spong bar byos, ‘you must give up’, for the Sanskrit's karoṣi, ‘you do’.

naṭavat, ‘like a performer’ (Tibetan gar mkhan bzhin du, ‘like a dancer’), shows Munidatta reading the song's naṛa (5b) as naṭa. The Tibetan translation of song line 5b reads it otherwise: khyod kyi ched du 'dam bu'i stan gzhag go, ‘for your sake I have laid down a seat of reeds’, taking naṛa as naḍa, ‘reed’. This bears on the draft of 5b rather than on the commentary. saṃsārapeṭaka, ‘the basket of saṃsāra’, is 'khor ba'i mdzod, ‘the treasury (or chest) of saṃsāra’, in the Tibetan.

ṣiṣayābhāsaṃ is a misprint for viṣayābhāsaṃ, as the glossary notes; the Tibetan yul gyi snang ba, ‘the appearance of objects’, confirms viṣaya. karoṣi(si): the parenthesis records the manuscript spelling karosi; translated through.

nairātmadharmasvarūpa: the Tibetan translation has chos thams cad bdag med pa'i ngo bo nyid, ‘the nature of the selflessness of all phenomena’, taking dharma as ‘phenomena’. I keep ‘the dharma of selflessness’, as in m1, but the Tibetan's sense is possible in both places. bhaga is transliterated in the Tibetan too (b+ha ga), supporting the keep-source policy. antareṇa is khyod kyi ched du, ‘for your sake’, supporting the draft's rendering of antare.

segments.translit:
pañcamapadena yogīndrasya saprapañcacaryyāmāha—
tuletyādi| bho ḍombi nairātme svarūpatayā tvāṃ bhadreṇa sadguruprasādāt jānāmi| haum̐ kāpālikaḥ| caryyādharaśca| kaṃ tava sukhaṃ pālituṃ samarthaḥ| ataeva tavāntareṇa mayā kṛṣṇācāryyeṇa ṣaṭtathāgatacakrīkuṇḍalakaṇṭhikādiniraṃśucaryyāṃ(yāṃ) vidhṛtya bāhyamantratantranirapekṣyatayā pañcava[18]rṇṇaviharaṇaṃ kṛtaṃ|
tathā ca kṛṣṇācāryyapādāḥ—
eku na kkijai manta na tanta
ṇiagharaṇī lai keli karanta|
naa gharem̐ gharaṇī jāva ṇa majjai
tāva ki pañcavāṇṇa viharijjai||
segments.translation: With the fifth [verse]{pada} he states the [conduct]{carya} with elaboration of the [lord of yogis]{yogindra}: “Hey you…” and so on. O [Ḍombī]{dombi}, [Nairātmā]{nairatma}, through the grace of the true [guru]{guru} I know you rightly, in your [true nature]{svarupa}. I am a [kāpālika]{kapalika} and one who keeps the [conduct]{carya}: able to guard ka, your bliss. That is why, for your sake, I, Master [Kāṇha]{p-kanha}, have taken up the unclothed [conduct]{carya} of the six [tathāgatas]{tathagata}' wheel, earrings, necklace and the rest, and, with no regard for outer mantras and tantras, have sported in the five colours. And so the revered Master [Kāṇha]{p-kanha}: “Not one thing is done, no mantra, no tantra: / taking one's own housewife, one makes love-play. / As long as the housewife in one's own house is not cleansed, / how can one sport in the five colours?”
segments.note: Munidatta says this verse shows the lord of yogis' conduct with elaboration. Knowing Nairātmā truly by the guru's grace, Kāṇha is a kāpālika: one able to guard (pāl-) ka, her bliss. For her sake he adopts the six tathāgatas' wheel, earrings and necklace, ignores outer mantras and tantras, and sports in ‘the five colours’ (the Tibetan: ‘five families’).

equations.en: one able to guard ka, that is, your bliss
Nairātmā

citations.quoted: eku na kkijai manta na tanta / ṇiagharaṇī lai keli karanta| / naa gharem̐ gharaṇī jāva ṇa majjai / tāva ki pañcavāṇṇa viharijjai||
citations.work: A dohā of Kṛṣṇācārya (Kāṇha), perhaps from his Dohākoṣa; Munidatta names the author but not the work

flags.note: niraṃśucaryyāṃ: niraṃśu is not a word as it stands. I take it as niraṃśuka, ‘unclothed’; niraṃśa, ‘partless’, is the other candidate. The Tibetan translation supports neither: where the Sanskrit has -kaṇṭhikādiniraṃśu-, it has de bzhin gshegs pa drug gi 'khor lo dang rna rgyan dang mgul rgyan dang rus rgyan gyi spyod pa, ‘the conduct of the wheel of the six tathāgatas, earrings, necklace and bone ornaments’, with rus rgyan, ‘bone ornaments’, and no word for nakedness. Probably corrupt; ‘unclothed’ is a guess.

pañcavarṇa (Apabhraṃśa pañcavāṇṇa), here and in the quoted verse: ‘five colours’ is literal; varṇa also means caste. The Tibetan translation has rigs lnga, ‘five families’ (also ‘five castes’; in tantric usage usually the five buddha families), in both the prose (rigs lnga'i spyod lam bya'o) and the verse, and no word for colour (kha dog). I keep ‘five colours’ pending a decision, but the Tibetan shows its translators did not read colours.

Apabhraṃśa verse: I now read naa gharem̐ as ṇia ghareṃ, ‘in one's own house’, because the Tibetan translation has rang khyim, ‘one's own house’ (before, the neutral ‘in the house’). For majjai the Tibetan has ma dag pa, ‘not purified’, so I now render ‘is not cleansed’ (majj- / mṛj-, ‘bathe, cleanse’) instead of ‘is not immersed’; ‘sinks, dissolves’ remains possible. The Tibetan makes line 1 conditional (gal te sngags rgyud cung zad cig med par, ‘if, with no mantra or tantra at all…’). kkijai = kijjai, ‘is done’.

kaṃ tava sukhaṃ pālituṃ samarthaḥ is a folk etymology of kapālī: ka (a lexical word for bliss) + pāl- ‘to guard’. The Tibetan translation keeps it in transliteration, kaM ni khyod kyi bde ba, pA ni skyong bar nus pa'o, ‘kaṃ is your bliss, pā is being able to guard’, which confirms the reading. It merges kāpālikaḥ caryādharaś ca into thod pa can gyi spyod pa 'dzin pa, ‘holding the conduct of a skull-bearer’.

saprapañcacaryām: ‘conduct with elaboration’. The Tibetan translation has spyod pa rab tu gsal bar gsungs, ‘explains the conduct very clearly’, taking saprapañca as describing the explanation. The printed compound favours my reading.

cakrī is the wheel ornament worn on the head; not linked to the glossary's ‘wheel’ entry, which is for the song-14 image. I take the six tathāgatas as governing the whole list of ornaments; the Tibetan (de bzhin gshegs pa drug gi 'khor lo dang…) can be read as ‘the wheel of the six tathāgatas’ only. nirapekṣyatayā for nirapekṣatayā. The Tibetan's bya'o, ‘shall do’, for kṛtaṃ, ‘has been done’, is not followed.

segments.translit:
ṣaṣṭhapadena ḍombinīdvidhābhedamāha—
saravaretyādi| gurusampradāyavihīnasya saiva ḍombinī apariśuddhāvadhūtikā sarovaraṃ kāyapuṣkaraṃ tanmūlaṃ tadeva bodhicittaṃ saṃvṛttyā śukrarūpaṃ mārayāmi| niḥsvabhāvīkaromi|
tathā ca bahiśāstre—
śā vittī kimpi jalaṃ yattu viśeṣeṇa gauravaṃ lahei|
ahimuha paḍia garalaṃ cchippi mutānaṃ kuṇeim̐|| 10||
segments.translation: With the sixth [verse]{pada} he states the twofold division of the [Ḍombī]{dombi}: “Breaking the [lake]{lake}…” and so on. For one who lacks the [guru's lineage]{guru-sampradaya}, that same [Ḍombī]{dombi} is the unpurified [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}. The [lake]{lake} is the pool of the body. Its root is that very [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}, which in [conventional]{samvrti} terms has the form of semen. This “I will kill”: I make it without intrinsic nature. And so in an outer treatise: “Water, even water hallowed with the Sāvitrī, gains its worth from the difference of the vessel: fallen into a snake's mouth it is poison; the oyster shell makes it pearls.”
segments.note: Munidatta says Ḍombī is twofold: for one lacking the guru's lineage she is the unpurified avadhūtī. The lake is the body's pool; its root is bodhicitta, conventionally semen, and ‘I will kill’ means making it without intrinsic nature. His proverb: water, even hallowed water, takes its worth from the vessel, poison in a snake's mouth, pearls in an oyster.

equations.en: the unpurified avadhūtī, for one who lacks the guru's lineage
the pool of the body (kāyapuṣkara)
bodhicitta, which in conventional terms has the form of semen
I make (it) without intrinsic nature

citations.quoted: śā vittī kimpi jalaṃ yattu viśeṣeṇa gauravaṃ lahei| ahimuha paḍia garalaṃ cchippi mutānaṃ kuṇeim̐||
citations.work: Unnamed ‘outer treatise’ (bahiḥśāstra); an unidentified Prakrit gnomic verse

flags.note: The Prakrit verse is corrupt, and the Tibetan translation helps: gang zhig sngags kyis byin brlabs chu / snod kyi khyad kyis bskur ba 'thob / sbrul gyi kha ru mid gyur na / nya phyis las skyugs mu tig gi, ‘whatever water is blessed by mantra gains honour through the difference of the vessel; if swallowed into a snake's mouth…; spat out from the oyster, of pearl’. On that evidence I now read śā vittī as sāvittī (Sanskrit sāvitrī, the Sāvitrī mantra; kimpi perhaps kiam pi, ‘even made’), yattu viśeṣeṇa as patta-viseseṇa (pātra, ‘vessel’; y/p confusion), cchippi as sippi, ‘oyster shell’, and mutānaṃ as muttāṇaṃ, ‘pearls’. ‘Poison’ (garalaṃ) is missing from the Tibetan. The Sāvitrī and the vessel are reconstructions.

Object of mārayāmi / niḥsvabhāvīkaromi: before, I supplied ‘her’ (Ḍombī, as in the song's mārami ḍombī). The printed text runs bodhicittaṃ … śukrarūpaṃ mārayāmi without a break, and the Tibetan translation runs on too (… khu ba'i ngo bos gsod pa ste / bdag gis rang bzhin med par byed pa'o), so I now take the bodhicitta as what is killed: ‘This “I will kill”: I make it without intrinsic nature.’ This diverges from the song, where Ḍombī is killed; not harmonized.

kāyapuṣkara: puṣkara is ‘lotus’ or ‘pond’; the Tibetan lus kyi rdzing bu, ‘the pond of the body’, takes it as a pool, so I now render ‘the pool of the body’ (before, ‘the lotus pool of the body’). tad eva, ‘that very’, is de bzhin nyid in the Tibetan, which usually means ‘suchness’; probably a literal rendering.

gurusampradāyavihīnasya is bla ma'i drin gyis rnam par dman pa in the Tibetan, with drin, ‘grace, kindness’, where m2 has man ngag, ‘instruction’; its syntax (‘deficient by the guru's grace’) is loose. bahiśāstre (for bahiḥśāstre), ‘in an outer treatise’: a work outside the tantric teaching (Tibetan phyi rol gyi bstan bcos); the Sāvitrī reading fits a brahmanical source. The closing ‘|| 10||’ is the song number and is not translated. The song's bhāñjīa (‘breaking’) and khāa (‘eats’) are not glossed.

questions: cp.10.m2: the printed asampradāyayogināṃ (‘of yogis who lack the lineage’) against the Tibetan's man ngag thob pa'i rnal 'byor pas (‘by the yogin who has obtained the instruction’), with no negation. I followed the Sanskrit and mention the Tibetan in the note. Should the negative stand?

boat: the glossary gives Munidatta's reading as ‘the path of conventional bodhicitta’. The Tibetan of m5 (kun rdzob byang chub kyi sems kyi gru'i lam gyis, ‘by the route of the boat of conventional bodhicitta’) supports ‘the boat is conventional bodhicitta, on whose route she comes and goes’. Revise the entry?

Divergences left unharmonized: 1b (Munidatta's ‘you go’, addressed to Nairātmā, against the song's ‘that brahmin goes’; the Tibetan has the same split); 3b (Kāṇha dances, against Ḍombī dances); 7b (on my revised reading of m8 he makes the bodhicitta, not Ḍombī, what is killed). How should these be signalled on the page? The 5a divergence I raised before (pallava against ‘baskets’) largely disappears with the Tibetan's ‘flower-stand’ and ‘petals’.

For the song draft: Munidatta's cittavaṭuka and the Tibetan song line's bram ze'i bu, ‘brahmin boy’, suggest that nāṛiā (1b, draft ‘shaven-headed’) was read as ‘lad, boy’; and the Tibetan of 5b has 'dam bu'i stan, ‘a seat of reeds’, reading naṛa as ‘reed’, where Munidatta reads naṭa, ‘performer’. Worth a look when the song is next revised?
pañcavarṇa (m7 and Kāṇha's verse): colours, castes, or, with the Tibetan rigs lnga, families? It may deserve an entry once decided.

nairātmadharma (m1, m6): the Tibetan has the abstract bdag med pa (not the goddess's bdag med ma) in both places, and in m6 ‘the selflessness of all phenomena’. Should the glossary move this form from nairatma to nairatmya, and should it be rendered ‘the dharma of selflessness’ or ‘the selflessness of phenomena’?

sandhya-bhasa and guru-sampradaya: the Tibetan renders the first as dgongs pa'i skad, ‘language of intention’ (sandhā), and the second as bla ma'i man ngag, ‘the guru's instruction’ (m2), and bla ma'i drin, ‘the guru's grace’ (m8). Keep ‘twilight language’ and ‘guru's lineage’?
m8 proverb: I adopted a reconstruction from the Tibetan (water hallowed with the Sāvitrī; worth from the vessel). Accept it, or mark the first line as unreadable?

Names: the glossary gives only ‘Kāṇha’ for p-kanha, so Munidatta's Kṛṣṇapāda is ‘Kāṇha’ and Kṛṣṇācārya ‘Master Kāṇha’; the Tibetan commentary has nag po spyod pa'i zhabs, nag po zhabs and nag po spyod pa pa. Should Kṛṣṇapāda and Kṛṣṇācārya be admitted as listed variants?

keep-source-first-gloss terms that first occur in the commentary (avadhūtī, Nairātmā, bodhicitta, siddha, Mahāmudrā, tathāgata, bhaga) get no first-occurrence note, because the 60-word notes have no room. Where should those glosses go?
